title: Diátaxis framework

provenance.license: Paraphrased; Diátaxis is CC BY-SA 4.0, attribution to diataxis.fr

verifyNote: Verify before relying: a paraphrase of the framework. See diataxis.fr for the full text.

items.title: Four types on two axes
items.text: Documentation divides into tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation, placed on two axes: whether it serves action or cognition, and whether it serves study or work. Tutorials serve action while studying; how-to guides serve action while working; reference serves cognition while working; explanation serves cognition while studying.

items.title: How-to guides
items.text: A how-to guide takes a competent reader through the steps to reach a stated goal. It states prerequisites without teaching them and handles the variations a working reader meets.

items.title: Tutorials
items.text: A tutorial takes a beginner from a stated starting point to a stated result along one path, and should work for every learner every time.

items.title: Reference
items.text: Reference describes the machinery (APIs, commands, options, settings) for a reader who consults it while working. It describes and nothing else: accurate, complete, neutral and austere, with no instruction, explanation or opinion beyond brief usage examples and necessary warnings. Its structure mirrors the structure of the product, and its entries follow one consistent pattern so readers find things where they expect them.

items.title: Explanation
items.text: Explanation deepens understanding for a reader who is studying rather than working: it gives context, background, history, reasons, design decisions, constraints and alternatives, and connects the topic to related ideas. It may hold opinion and perspective, and weighs alternatives openly. It needs a boundary (often framed as "About <topic>" or a why question) and leaves step-by-step instruction and technical description to how-to guides and reference.

title: IDEA discipline and behavior (34 CFR 300.530, 300.324(a)(2)(i))

provenance.source: 34 CFR 300.530 (authority of school personnel) and 300.324(a)(2)(i) (positive behavioral interventions)
provenance.license: Paraphrased summary (source: public domain US government)

verifyNote: Verify before relying: agency rules change, and state rules (for example on restraint and time-out) apply on top. Check the source for the current version.

items.title: Positive behavioral interventions
items.text: When a student's behavior impedes the student's learning or that of others, the IEP team considers positive behavioral interventions and supports, and other strategies, to address that behavior.

items.title: Removals of up to 10 school days
items.text: School personnel may remove a student with a disability who violates a code of conduct for up to 10 consecutive school days, to the extent those options apply to students without disabilities, and for further removals of up to 10 days for separate incidents that do not amount to a change of placement.

items.title: Services after 10 days of removal
items.text: After a student has been removed for 10 school days in the same school year, services are provided during later removals so the student can keep taking part in the general curriculum, in another setting, and progress toward the IEP goals.

items.title: FBA and behavioral intervention during removal
items.text: A student removed under the change-of-placement or special-circumstances provisions receives, as appropriate, a functional behavioral assessment and behavioral intervention services and modifications designed to address the behavior so it does not recur.

items.title: Manifestation determination
items.text: Within 10 school days of any decision to change the placement of a student with a disability because of a code-of-conduct violation, the agency, the parent and relevant members of the IEP team review the relevant information and decide whether the conduct was caused by, or had a direct and substantial relationship to, the disability, or was the direct result of the agency's failure to implement the IEP.

items.title: FBA and plan when the conduct is a manifestation
items.text: When the conduct is found to be a manifestation of the disability, the IEP team conducts a functional behavioral assessment (unless one was done before the behavior that led to the change of placement) and implements a behavioral intervention plan, or, when a plan already exists, reviews it and modifies it as needed to address the behavior.

items.title: Return to placement
items.text: Except in the special circumstances, a student whose conduct was a manifestation returns to the placement from which the student was removed, unless the parent and the agency agree to a change as part of modifying the behavioral intervention plan.

items.title: Special circumstances
items.text: For weapons, illegal drugs or controlled substances, or serious bodily injury at school, on school premises or at a school function, school personnel may remove the student to an interim alternative educational setting for up to 45 school days whether or not the behavior is a manifestation.

items.title: State rules apply on top
items.text: States set their own rules on restraint, time-out and related notices to parents, which apply in addition to these federal rules. See the state's rules (in Texas, 19 TAC §89.1053).

title: IDEA evaluation, reevaluation and eligibility (34 CFR 300.300, 300.303–300.306)

provenance.license: Paraphrased summary (source: public domain US government)

verifyNote: Verify before relying: agency rules change. Check the source for the current version.

items.title: All areas assessed
items.text: Every area related to the suspected disability is assessed, including where appropriate health, vision, hearing, social and emotional status, general intelligence, academic performance, communicative status and motor abilities.

items.title: A variety of sources
items.text: The evaluation uses a variety of assessment tools and strategies to gather functional, developmental and academic information, including information from the parent.

items.title: No single measure decides
items.text: No single measure or assessment is the sole basis for deciding whether the student has a disability or for designing the educational program.

items.title: Valid, unbiased administration
items.text: Assessments are chosen and given without racial or cultural bias, in the student's language and form of communication most likely to yield accurate information, used only for purposes for which they are valid and reliable, given by trained personnel, and given as the publisher directs.

items.title: All needs identified
items.text: The evaluation is comprehensive enough to identify all of the student's special education and related service needs, whether or not they are commonly linked to the suspected category.

items.title: Exclusionary factors
items.text: A student is not found eligible when the determinant factor is lack of appropriate instruction in reading or math, or limited English proficiency.

items.title: When a reevaluation happens
items.text: A student with a disability is reevaluated when the agency decides the student's educational or related services needs, including academic achievement and functional performance, call for it, or when the parent or a teacher asks for one.

items.title: Not more than once a year
items.text: A reevaluation happens no more than once a year unless the parent and the agency agree otherwise.

items.title: Reevaluation at least every three years
items.text: A reevaluation happens at least once every three years unless the parent and the agency agree it is unnecessary.

items.title: Review of existing evaluation data
items.text: As part of any reevaluation, the IEP team and other qualified professionals review the existing data: evaluations and information from the parent; current classroom-based, local or state assessments and classroom-based observations; and observations by teachers and related services providers.

items.title: What additional data, if any, is needed
items.text: From that review and the parent's input, the group identifies what additional data, if any, it needs to decide: whether the student continues to have a disability and what the student's educational needs are; the present levels of academic achievement and related developmental needs; whether the student continues to need special education and related services; and whether additions or changes to the services are needed for the student to meet the IEP's annual goals and take part, as appropriate, in the general curriculum.

items.title: Review may be held without a meeting
items.text: The group may review the existing data without holding a meeting.

items.title: Assessments to produce the data
items.text: The agency gives the assessments and other measures needed to produce the additional data the group identified.

items.title: Notice when no additional data is needed
items.text: When the group decides no additional data is needed to decide continued eligibility and educational needs, the agency tells the parent of that decision and the reasons for it, and of the parent's right to ask for an assessment anyway. The agency need not assess unless the parent asks.

items.title: Evaluation before ending eligibility
items.text: Before deciding a student no longer has a disability, the agency evaluates the student, except when eligibility ends through graduation with a regular diploma or by aging out; in those cases the student receives a summary of academic achievement and functional performance with recommendations for postsecondary goals.

items.title: Consent for reevaluation
items.text: The agency obtains informed parental consent before reevaluating, unless it can show it made reasonable efforts to obtain consent and the parent did not respond. If the parent refuses, the agency may, but need not, pursue the reevaluation through the consent override procedures.

items.title: Reviewing existing data needs no consent
items.text: Parental consent is not required before reviewing existing data as part of an evaluation or reevaluation.

title: IDEA individualized education program (34 CFR 300.320–300.324)

provenance.source: 34 CFR 300.320 (IEP contents), 300.321 (IEP team), 300.322 (parent participation), 300.323 (when IEPs must be in effect), 300.324 (development, review and revision)
provenance.license: Paraphrased summary (source: public domain US government)

verifyNote: Verify before relying: agency rules change. Check the source for the current version.

items.title: Present levels of performance
items.text: The IEP states the student's present levels of academic achievement and functional performance, including how the disability affects involvement and progress in the general education curriculum (for a preschool child, participation in appropriate activities).

items.title: Measurable annual goals
items.text: The IEP states measurable annual goals, academic and functional, that meet the needs resulting from the disability so the student can be involved in and progress in the general curriculum, and that meet each of the student's other disability-related educational needs.

items.title: Benchmarks for alternate assessment
items.text: For a student who takes alternate assessments aligned to alternate achievement standards, the IEP also describes benchmarks or short-term objectives.

items.title: How and when progress is reported
items.text: The IEP describes how progress toward each annual goal will be measured and when periodic reports on that progress will be given (for example quarterly, or with report cards).

items.title: Services, aids and supports
items.text: The IEP states the special education and related services and supplementary aids and services, based on peer-reviewed research to the extent practicable, and the program modifications or supports for school personnel, that will let the student advance toward the goals, progress in the general curriculum, take part in extracurricular and nonacademic activities, and be educated with other students with and without disabilities.

items.title: Start date, frequency, location and duration
items.text: For each service and modification, the IEP gives the projected start date and the anticipated frequency, location and duration.

items.title: Participation with nondisabled peers
items.text: The IEP explains the extent, if any, to which the student will not take part with nondisabled students in the regular class and in extracurricular and nonacademic activities.

items.title: State and district assessments
items.text: The IEP lists individual accommodations needed on state and districtwide assessments; when the team decides on an alternate assessment, it states why the student cannot take the regular assessment and why the chosen alternate assessment is appropriate.

items.title: Transition services
items.text: Beginning not later than the first IEP in effect when the student turns 16 (younger if the team decides), and updated each year, the IEP includes measurable postsecondary goals based on age-appropriate transition assessments for training, education, employment and, where appropriate, independent living, and the transition services, including courses of study, needed to reach them. States may set an earlier age.

items.title: Transfer of rights at the age of majority
items.text: Beginning at least one year before the student reaches the state's age of majority, the IEP states that the student has been told of the rights that will transfer at that age.

items.title: IEP team
items.text: The team includes the parents; at least one regular education teacher if the student is or may be in the regular environment; at least one special education teacher or provider; an agency representative who can provide or supervise specially designed instruction and knows the curriculum and resources; someone who can interpret the instructional implications of evaluation results; others with knowledge of the student at the parent's or agency's discretion; and the student when appropriate (always invited when transition is discussed).

items.title: Parent participation
items.text: The agency takes steps so that one or both parents attend or have the opportunity to take part: notice early enough, a mutually agreed time and place, other ways to take part when they cannot attend, an interpreter when needed, and a copy of the IEP at no cost. A meeting held without a parent requires records of the attempts to arrange one.

items.title: Initial IEP meeting
items.text: The meeting to develop the initial IEP is held within 30 days of the determination that the student needs special education and related services; services are made available as soon as possible after the IEP is developed.

items.title: IEP accessible to those who carry it out
items.text: Each teacher and provider responsible for carrying out the IEP can see it and is told of their specific responsibilities and the specific accommodations, modifications and supports it requires.

items.title: What the team considers
items.text: In developing the IEP the team considers the student's strengths, the parents' concerns for enhancing the student's education, the results of the initial or most recent evaluation, and the student's academic, developmental and functional needs.

items.title: Special factors
items.text: The team considers positive behavioral interventions and supports when behavior impedes the student's learning or that of others; the language needs of a student with limited English proficiency; Braille instruction for a student who is blind or visually impaired unless the evaluation shows it is not appropriate; the communication needs of every student, including language and communication mode for a student who is deaf or hard of hearing; and whether the student needs assistive technology devices and services.

items.title: Annual review
items.text: The team reviews the IEP periodically, and at least once a year, to decide whether the annual goals are being achieved, and revises it to address lack of expected progress, reevaluation results, information from or to the parents, anticipated needs or other matters.

items.title: Amending without a meeting
items.text: After the annual meeting, the parent and the agency may agree to change the IEP by a written amendment instead of a meeting; the team is told of the change and the parent receives a revised copy on request.

title: NIH policies on AI and award decisions

provenance.source: NOT-OD-25-132, NOT-OD-23-149 and the unified NIH funding strategy (summarized in docs/workflows-by-document-type.md)
provenance.license: Paraphrased summary (source: public domain US government)

verifyNote: Verify before relying: agency rules change. Check the source for the current version.

items.title: AI and application originality (NOT-OD-25-132)
items.text: From September 25, 2025, NIH does not treat applications, or sections, substantially developed by AI as the applicant's original ideas.

items.title: Generative AI in peer review (NOT-OD-23-149)
items.text: NIH peer reviewers may not put applications they review into generative AI tools. A mock review is for the applicant's own draft only.

items.title: No paylines
items.text: Since the January 2026 council round, NIH institutes do not rely on paylines. Report scores and weaknesses and make no award prediction from a cutoff.

title: NIH page limits: Specific Aims and Research Strategy

provenance.license: Paraphrased summary (source: public domain US government)

verifyNote: Verify before relying: agency rules change. Check the source for the current version.

items.title: Specific Aims
items.text: Specific Aims is limited to 1 page.

items.title: Research Strategy (R01, R15, U01)
items.text: Research Strategy is limited to 12 pages for R01, R15 and U01 applications.

items.title: Research Strategy (R03, R21)
items.text: Research Strategy is limited to 6 pages for R03 and R21 applications.

items.title: Introduction to a resubmission or revision
items.text: The Introduction to a resubmission or revision application is limited to 1 page for all activity codes; resubmissions of institutional training and related programs (T, D43, D71, U2R, K12, KL2, R25, UE5, R38, DP7) allow 3 pages. It summarizes substantial additions, deletions and changes and responds to the issues and criticism in the summary statement. Changes are outlined only in the Introduction, not marked up in the application.

items.title: The NOFO governs
items.text: These limits apply unless the funding opportunity (NOFO) says otherwise.

title: NIH simplified peer review framework

provenance.source: NIH simplified peer review framework and first-level review scoring (summarized in docs/workflows-by-document-type.md)
provenance.license: Paraphrased summary (source: public domain US government)

verifyNote: Verify before relying: agency rules change. Check the source for the current version.

items.title: Factor 1: Importance of the Research
items.text: Covers Significance and Innovation. Scored from 1 to 9.

items.title: Factor 2: Rigor and Feasibility
items.text: Covers the Approach, including controls, sample size justification, the analysis plan, biological variables such as sex or age, pitfalls and alternatives, and the timeline. Scored from 1 to 9.

items.title: Factor 3: Expertise and Resources
items.text: Rated sufficient or gaps identified, not scored.

items.title: Overall Impact
items.text: Reviewers give an Overall Impact score from 1 to 9, where 1 is best. The framework covers most research project grants with due dates from January 25, 2025.

title: NSF PAPPG 24-1 (with Supplement 2): Project Description, merit review and DMSP

provenance.source: NSF PAPPG 24-1 Ch. II.D.2 and Ch. III.A; PAPPG 24-1 Supplement 2 (NSF 26-202, effective January 22, 2026); NSF ENG DMSP guidance; NSF updates on priorities
provenance.license: Paraphrased summary (source: public domain US government)

verifyNote: Verify before relying: NSF has deferred a new PAPPG and issues changes by supplemental notice. The solicitation governs where it differs from the PAPPG.

items.title: The solicitation governs
items.text: A program solicitation's instructions take precedence over the PAPPG where the two differ, including page limits and DMSP requirements. Supplement 2 (NSF 26-202) takes precedence over the PAPPG 24-1 base text where they conflict.

items.title: Project Description page limit
items.text: The Project Description, including Results from Prior NSF Support, may not exceed 15 pages. Charts, graphs, maps and photographs count toward the limit. Going over needs a deviation authorized in advance.

items.title: Self-contained, no URLs
items.text: The Project Description must be self-contained and must not use URLs.

items.title: Broader Impacts section heading
items.text: The Project Description must contain a separate section with "Broader Impacts" as a heading on its own line. Broader impacts may come from the research itself, from activities tied directly to the research, or from complementary activities the project supports.

items.title: What the Project Description states
items.text: The objectives for the period of the award and their expected significance; how the work relates to the current state of knowledge and to the PI's work under other support; the general plan of work, including the broad design and, where appropriate, methods and procedures; and, in brief, what the project will do, why, how, how success will be known and what benefits could follow.

items.title: When Results from Prior NSF Support are required
items.text: Each PI and co-PI who has an NSF award that ended in the past five years, or any current NSF funding (including no-cost extensions and salary support), reports on one award: the one most closely related to the proposal.

items.title: Results from Prior NSF Support page limit
items.text: Results from Prior NSF Support may take up to five pages, which count toward the 15-page Project Description.

items.title: What Results from Prior NSF Support contain
items.text: The award number, amount and period of support; the project title; a summary of results with Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts under two separate headings; the publications from the award (or a statement that there were none); evidence of research products and their availability as described in the data plan; and, for a renewal, how the completed work relates to the proposed work. A recent award with no results yet describes its major goals and broader impacts instead.

items.title: Project Summary (outside the Project Description)
items.text: A full proposal also needs a Project Summary of no more than one page in three parts: Overview, Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts. It is not an abstract and should be understandable to a broad scientific audience.

items.title: Merit review criterion: Intellectual Merit
items.text: The potential to advance knowledge.

items.title: Merit review criterion: Broader Impacts
items.text: The potential to benefit society and contribute to specific, desired societal outcomes.

items.title: Review element 1: potential
items.text: Applied to both criteria: the potential of the activity to advance knowledge within or across fields (Intellectual Merit) and to benefit society or advance desired societal outcomes (Broader Impacts).

items.title: Review element 2: creative and original concepts
items.text: How far the activities suggest and explore creative, original or potentially transformative concepts.

items.title: Review element 3: a sound plan with a way to assess success
items.text: Whether the plan is well reasoned, well organized and based on a sound rationale, and includes a mechanism to assess success.

items.title: Review element 4: qualifications
items.text: How well qualified the individual, team or organization is to carry out the activities.

items.title: Review element 5: resources
items.text: Whether adequate resources are available to the PI, at the home organization or through collaborations, to carry out the activities.

items.title: DMSP built in the Research.gov tool
items.text: Proposals must include a Data Management and Sharing Plan (DMSP) created with the Research.gov tool, released April 27, 2026; proposals submitted before that date used a PDF upload. Check the tool and the solicitation for any length limit: NSF 26-202 and NSF Engineering's guidance still refer to a two-page limit, and a solicitation may set its own requirements or exceptions. The DMSP is not part of the 15-page Project Description; data management material that does not fit in the plan may use part of the 15-page Project Description, but the DMSP must not be used to get around the Project Description page limit. Proposals without a DMSP are returned without review.
items.citation: PAPPG 24-1 Ch. II.D.2 as revised by NSF 26-202

items.title: DMSP tool fields
items.text: For each data or research product category, the tool asks for: data or research product category; access policies and limitations; data standards and metadata; data or research product provenance; public archiving; timeline for public accessibility; data availability; and accountability (the senior personnel responsible for the plan). Listed in NSF Engineering's guidance (updated July 2026); the prompts may vary by directorate, so check the live form.

items.title: Data behind publications shared at publication
items.text: Recipients share all data supporting NSF-funded publications at the time of publication. Any exception must be described and justified in the DMSP at the original submission.

items.title: One DMSP for a collaborative proposal
items.text: Simultaneously submitted collaborative proposals, and proposals with subawards, carry one combined DMSP.

items.title: No detailed plan needs a justification
items.text: A DMSP may say that no detailed plan is needed, but only with a clear justification.

items.title: The DMSP is reviewed
items.text: The DMSP is reviewed as part of the proposal under Intellectual Merit, Broader Impacts or both. Directorate or program-specific DMSP requirements apply where they exist.

items.title: Participation activities open to all
items.text: NSF's priorities statement (April 18, 2025) says broadening participation and outreach activities, including Broader Impacts work, must be open and available to all Americans and must not preference or exclude people on the basis of protected characteristics, directly or indirectly.

title: Texas FIE timelines (19 TAC §89.1011)

provenance.source: 19 TAC §89.1011, Full Individual and Initial Evaluation, as amended effective July 30, 2024 (49 TexReg 5515); no later amendment found on 2026-10-08. Summarized in docs/workflows-by-document-type.md
provenance.license: Paraphrased summary (source: Texas Administrative Code, public law)

verifyNote: Verify before relying: agency rules change. Check the source for the current version.

items.title: Referral
items.text: Referral for an initial evaluation is part of the district's multi-tiered system of supports. A district may not require a set period of intervention before referral, refers when difficulties continue or a disability is suspected, and keeps providing supports while the evaluation is under way.

items.title: Response to a parent's written request
items.text: Not later than the 15th school day after receiving a parent's written request for an evaluation, the district gives prior written notice of the proposed evaluation with the procedural safeguards notice, the agency's parent overview and an opportunity to consent, or prior written notice of its refusal with the same notices.

items.title: Written FIE report
items.text: The written report is due by the 45th school day after the district receives written consent. When the student is absent three or more school days in that period, the deadline is extended by the number of school days missed.

items.title: End-of-year exceptions
items.text: When consent is received at least 35 but fewer than 45 school days before the last instructional day of the school year, the report goes to the parent by June 30 (unless the student is absent three or more days in that period, when the usual timeline applies). When consent is received fewer than 35 school days before the last instructional day, the usual timeline applies. See source for the details.

items.title: ARD committee decision
items.text: The ARD committee makes its eligibility decision within 30 calendar days of the date the written report is completed. If that day falls in the summer, the committee meets by the 15th school day of the next school year, or sooner when the report shows a need for extended school year services.

items.title: Parent copy of the report
items.text: The parent receives a copy of the report as soon as possible after it is completed and at least five school days before the initial ARD meeting (by June 30 under the end-of-year exception).

items.title: What counts as a school day
items.text: For these timelines, school days do not include days between the last instructional day of the spring term and the first instructional day of the fall term.

title: Texas eligibility criteria (19 TAC §89.1040)

provenance.source: 19 TAC §89.1040, Eligibility Criteria, as amended effective October 4, 2026 (adopted 51 TexReg, September 25, 2026 issue; earlier text at Cornell LII). Summarized in docs/workflows-by-document-type.md
provenance.license: Paraphrased summary (source: Texas Administrative Code, public law)

verifyNote: Verify before relying: the 2026 amendments changed the intellectual disability and developmental delay criteria and added a validity requirement. Check the current rule text, and swap this set for your state's criteria outside Texas.

items.title: Who decides
items.text: The student's ARD committee decides eligibility, after an evaluation that follows 34 CFR 300.301–300.306. The evaluation group includes a school psychologist, an educational diagnostician or another appropriately certified or licensed practitioner with experience and training in the area of the disability, or a licensed or certified professional for the specific category.

items.title: Factors affecting validity
items.text: The evaluation report includes any situations, conditions or circumstances that might affect the validity of the instruments or assessments used (added in 2026).

items.title: Autism
items.text: The student meets the federal definition of autism (34 CFR 300.8(c)(1)). A medical or psychological diagnosis is not required, and the absence of some associated characteristics does not rule it out. The evaluation report includes recommendations on communication, social interaction and positive behavioral interventions and supports. See source for the full criteria.

items.title: Deaf-blindness
items.text: Based on the hearing and vision evaluations, the student meets both the deaf or hard of hearing and the visual impairment criteria; or meets the visual impairment criteria with a suspected hearing loss that cannot be shown conclusively and no speech at the age speech would normally be expected; or has losses that together adversely affect educational performance; or has a documented progressive medical condition that will result in both. See source for the full criteria.

items.title: Deaf or hard of hearing
items.text: The student meets the federal criteria for deafness or hearing impairment. The data include an audiological evaluation by a licensed audiologist, a communication assessment, and a description of how the hearing loss affects hearing in different situations with or without amplification. See source for the full criteria and the rules for children under three.

items.title: Emotional disability
items.text: The student meets the federal criteria for emotional disturbance (34 CFR 300.8(c)(4)). The evaluation report includes recommendations for positive behavioral supports and interventions. See source for the full criteria.

items.title: Intellectual disability
items.text: Significantly subaverage intellectual functioning, shown either by an overall score at least two standard deviations below the mean on a standardized, individually administered cognitive test (allowing for the standard error of measurement), or, after a cognitive test was attempted or completed and the team explains why standardized cognitive measures are invalid, inaccessible or inappropriate, by a convergence of evidence from multiple direct and indirect sources; and, concurrently, deficits in at least two areas of adaptive behavior. See source for the full criteria (amended 2026).

items.title: Multiple disabilities
items.text: A combination of disabilities under this section, expected to continue indefinitely, that severely impairs performance in at least two of: psychomotor skills, self-care, communication, social and emotional development, or cognition. A student with more than one disability who does not meet this is not reported as having multiple disabilities, and deaf-blindness is excluded. See source for the full criteria.

items.title: Orthopedic impairment
items.text: The student meets the federal criteria for orthopedic impairment, and the eligibility determination includes a medical diagnosis by a licensed physician. See source for the full criteria.

items.title: Other health impairment
items.text: The student meets the federal criteria for other health impairment (a chronic or acute health problem that limits strength, vitality or alertness and adversely affects educational performance), and a licensed physician, a physician assistant or an advanced practice registered nurse with delegated authority identifies or confirms the health problem. See source for the full criteria.

items.title: Specific learning disability
items.text: Determined with a variety of assessment tools; the student does not achieve adequately for age or grade level in one or more of oral expression, listening comprehension, written expression, basic reading skill, reading fluency, reading comprehension, math calculation or math problem solving, shown by multiple measures, despite appropriate instruction; and either does not make sufficient progress with scientific, research-based intervention or shows a pattern of strengths and weaknesses relevant to the disability. A significant variance among specific areas of cognitive function, or between cognitive function and achievement, is not required. The team considers data showing appropriate instruction in reading or math by qualified staff and repeated assessments of achievement at reasonable intervals shared with the parents, and the student is observed in the learning environment, including the general education classroom. See source for the full criteria, team membership, and the dyslexia and dysgraphia provisions.

items.title: Specific learning disability: further exclusions
items.text: The learning difficulties must not be primarily the result of a visual, hearing or motor disability; intellectual disability; emotional disability; cultural factors; environmental or economic disadvantage; or being an emergent bilingual student.

items.title: Speech impairment
items.text: The student meets the federal criteria for speech or language impairment, and the multidisciplinary team includes a certified speech and hearing therapist, a certified speech and language therapist or a licensed speech-language pathologist. See source for the full criteria.

items.title: Traumatic brain injury
items.text: The student meets the federal criteria for traumatic brain injury, and the eligibility determination includes a medical diagnosis by a licensed physician. See source for the full criteria.

items.title: Visual impairment
items.text: The student meets the federal criteria for visual impairment. The data include a medical report from a licensed ophthalmologist or optometrist with visual acuity and field measurements, a functional vision evaluation, a learning media assessment by a certified teacher of students with visual impairments, and, for the initial evaluation, an orientation and mobility evaluation; a certified orientation and mobility specialist takes part in eligibility decisions. See source for the full criteria.

items.title: Developmental delay
items.text: For a student aged three through nine evaluated for at least one other category, with evidence of a suspected disability that cannot yet be confirmed: a delay in physical, cognitive, communication, social or emotional, or adaptive development, shown by multiple converging sources (including an Early Childhood Intervention evaluation where applicable) as at least two standard deviations below the mean in one area, at least 1.5 standard deviations below the mean in two or more areas, or a documented history and pattern of atypical development. Districts are not required to use this category. See source for the full criteria.

items.title: Noncategorical early childhood
items.text: Students aged three through five evaluated as having intellectual disability, emotional disability, specific learning disability or autism could be described as noncategorical early childhood; districts may no longer use this description for new identifications from the 2025–2026 school year. See source for the transition rules.

title: Federal award reporting: 2 CFR 200 performance reports, prior approvals and agency report formats
authority: Office of Management and Budget (2 CFR Part 200); NIH; NSF

provenance.source: 2 CFR 200.308, 200.328 and 200.329 (eCFR, current as of 2026-10-07; sections last amended 2024-10-01); NIH RPPR reporting requirements; NSF project reporting
provenance.license: Paraphrased summary (source: public domain US government)

verifyNote: Verify before relying: the award's terms and conditions set the report format and due dates and override these defaults. Foundations set their own formats.

items.title: Accomplishments compared with the award's objectives
items.text: As applicable, a performance report compares accomplishments with the objectives the award set for the reporting period, explains why established goals or objectives were not met, and explains cost overruns or higher-than-expected unit costs.

items.title: Relate financial data and accomplishments to the goals
items.text: When reporting performance, the recipient relates financial data and accomplishments to the performance goals and objectives of the award, and gives cost information (such as unit costs) when the award's terms require it. For discretionary research awards this may be limited to technical performance reports. Agencies use OMB-approved common forms such as the Research Performance Progress Report (RPPR).

items.title: How often performance reports are due
items.text: Performance reports are due as the award requires, no less often than annually and no more often than quarterly unless specific conditions apply.

items.title: Annual performance report: federal default
items.text: An annual report is due no later than 90 calendar days after the reporting period, unless the agency requires annual reports before the anniversary dates of a multi-year award (as NIH and NSF do).

items.title: Quarterly or semiannual performance report
items.text: A quarterly or semiannual report is due no later than 30 calendar days after the reporting period.

items.title: Final performance report
items.text: The recipient's final performance report is due no later than 120 calendar days after the period of performance ends (90 days for a subrecipient reporting to a pass-through entity). The agency may extend a due date with justification.

items.title: Significant developments between reports
items.text: Problems, delays or adverse conditions that will affect milestones or objectives, and developments that allow meeting them sooner, at lower cost or with different beneficial results, are reported to the agency when they occur. A negative development comes with a corrective action plan and any help needed.

items.title: Financial reports
items.text: Financial reporting uses OMB-approved data elements (currently the SF-425), at least annually and at most quarterly. Annual financial reports are due within 90 calendar days of the period, quarterly or semiannual within 30, and the final within 120 days of the end of the period of performance. Numbers in the performance report should agree with them.

items.title: Deviations reported, prior approval requested
items.text: Deviations from the approved budget, scope or objectives are reported in the performance report, and the revisions that need prior approval are requested from the agency or pass-through entity.

items.title: Prior approval: change in scope or objective
items.text: A change in the scope or objective of the project needs prior written approval, even with no budget change.

items.title: Prior approval: key personnel and PI effort
items.text: A change in key personnel named in the award needs prior written approval, as does the PI's disengagement for more than three months or a 25 percent reduction in the PI's time and effort over the period of performance.

items.title: Prior approval: budget changes
items.text: Prior written approval is also needed to move participant support funds to other categories, to add subaward work not in the approved application, to change the approved cost-sharing amount, for additional federal funds, and to move funds between construction and non-construction work. Agencies may restrict transfers among direct cost categories over 10 percent of the total budget on awards above the simplified acquisition threshold.

items.title: No-cost extensions
items.text: Where the award allows, a recipient may start a one-time extension of up to 12 months by notifying the agency in writing at least 10 calendar days before the period ends; it needs prior approval when the terms prohibit it, it needs more federal funds, or it changes the approved scope. Other no-cost extensions need prior approval, requested at least 10 calendar days before the end.

items.title: NIH: Research Performance Progress Report
items.text: NIH uses the RPPR. Annual SNAP RPPRs are due about 45 days before the next budget period starts, non-SNAP about 60 days before, and multi-year funded RPPRs annually on or before the anniversary; the final RPPR is due 120 days after the end of the period of performance. Check exact dates in eRA Commons.

items.title: NSF: annual, final and project outcomes reports
items.text: NSF annual project reports are due no later than 90 days before the end of the current budget period and are submitted in Research.gov. The final annual report covers only the last year and is due within 120 days of the award's end date, as is the Project Outcomes Report: no more than 800 words, for a public audience, posted as submitted.
